title: Can luxury save Macy's?
summary: This week's celebration of Macy's 100th Thanksgiving parade finds the department store at a turning point. After years of losing sales, the retailer is reimagining itself — as a higher-end destination.
text:
Can luxury save Macy's?
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."
As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.
As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.

title: The stories we’re grateful for this year
summary: STAT staffers have put together a list of the stories we’re thankful for this year — check out our favorites.
text:
Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Hope everyone is enjoying their food coma after yesterday. What was your favorite dish? I am still thinking about my friend’s pumpkin pie.
Speaking of the holiday, STAT staffers have put together a list of the stories we’re thankful for this year. Scroll down to see our favorites.
Doctors keep missing the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders
Anorexia, binge eating, and other disorders can emerge before and after childbirth, but the women who struggle with them often slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system.
Research is limited, but we do know a few things: About 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders. Women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns. And obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions or how to use the few screening tools we have validated for eating disorders in pregnancy.
Read more about the gap in this research.
Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes spell trouble for specialists
In the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians, the agency cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when the services are provided by the same physician or practice.
A bit wonky, I know, but it’s part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.
What does this mean? Opponents say the policy change will force patients to return for separate appointments and increase out-of-pocket costs and wait times. People with Parkinson’s disease, for example, could struggle to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain. Read more.

title: Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
summary: Medicare’s zero-premium drug plans are disappearing, millions are losing their plans, and the average prescription drug plan premium could rise 50% if you stay put. Here’s what to check.
text:
Medicare Open Enrollment: Here’s What’s Changing, and What Mistakes To Avoid
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn’t one plan. It’s more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there’s no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn’t cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
“People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs,” said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The Hassle Saves Money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It’s a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can’t find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn’t tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.

title: My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
summary: Solo-dining is being embraced as a self-care trend and it's reshaping the restaurant industry.
text:
My self-care ritual is a meal at a fancy restaurant - on my own
- Published
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.
"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.
The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.
As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."
We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.
Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.
She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.
"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.
"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."
Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".
"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."
Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.
Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.
Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.
"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.
"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."
A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.
"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.
Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

title: How Jensen Huang's return as NVIDIA's CEO is going over in China
summary: In China, Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO is being met with a mixed reaction – as Beijing weighs whether it wants the US company's chips at all.
text:
How Jensen Huang's return as NVIDIA's CEO is going over in China
In China, Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO is being met with a mixed reaction – as Beijing weighs whether it wants the US company's chips at all.
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:
Jensen Huang now has his job back at NVIDIA. Whether China should have access to NVIDIA's best computer chips - that debate is now back, too. And how is all this playing out in China? Well, we've reached NPR's Jennifer Pak in Beijing. Hi there.
JENNIFER PAK, BYLINE: Hi.
SUMMERS: Jennifer, you're there in Beijing. Tell us what you've been hearing from people.
PAK: Well, from the general public, some say this whole saga of Jensen Huang's swift fall and sudden return is kind of like a microdrama. I don't know if you're familiar with these. These are super popular, kind of like soap operas. They're broken down into bite-size episodes, two to three minutes each, super fast pace. And just like a microdrama, this Huang scandal has had a lot of twists and turns.
In China's tech circles, the views are split. I spoke to Du Chen, a technology media editor at Ifanr in Beijing. He says one group believes Huang's conduct raises serious ethical violations and shouldn't be in charge. While the other group, he says, are ones who have had business dealings with NVIDIA or interacted with Huang directly and indirectly.
DU CHEN: (Speaking Chinese).
PAK: This group, he says, generally trusts Huang's ability as the company's CEO and believes he would return, just not as fast as it happened, like 11 days.
SUMMERS: It was really fast, yeah. Now, what about the allegation that China launched a spy operation targeting NVIDIA and Huang? Has there been much discussion about that?

title: Pregnancy is the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders, but doctors keep missing them
summary: Many women struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth, but they often slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system.
text:
Reporting for this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.
REISTERSTOWN, Md. — Katye Jorgensen had been fighting anorexia and bulimia for years when she got pregnant at 25. Weigh-ins at prenatal appointments filled her with dread and certain foods terrified her, but she powered through for her baby’s sake. Then she struggled to breastfeed her son and lose weight after giving birth, and her mental health deteriorated.
After her second pregnancy two years later, Jorgensen became obsessive about exercise and fixated on comments about how well she was “bouncing back.” At her husband’s urging, she started seeing a therapist and a dietitian. Eventually, they staged an intervention and she agreed to enter intensive treatment, which she said saved her life.
“I went to my postpartum appointment, I mentioned a lot of this, and even though I really liked those doctors, it still didn’t set off any red alarms for anybody,” said Jorgensen, who is now 37.
Jorgensen is one of many women who struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth but slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system. Research suggests about 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or binge eating disorder, though research is limited and no one knows their exact toll.
Those rates are on par with national averages: an estimated 2.6% to 8.4% of women will experience an eating disorder over their lifetimes — that’s up to 14.6 million women and girls in the United States.
Eating disorders have been linked to health issues for pregnant women — including miscarriage, high blood pressure, anemia, and bleeding — and complications for their developing babies, including small head circumference, low birthweight, autism, and asthma. After birth, women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns.
The risks vary by eating disorder. Studies don’t prove that eating disorders directly cause these issues and not everyone with a perinatal eating disorder will experience them. Still, the evidence is enough to worry clinicians.
“If we don’t treat these disorders … there are risks involved there. This isn’t a neutral situation,” said Leah Graves, a registered dietitian and a clinical adviser at the National Eating Disorders Association.
Few screening tools have been validated for eating disorders in pregnancy, and none are widely used. Obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions, leaving them unequipped to identify or manage eating disorders. And even with a diagnosis, many pregnant women and new mothers don’t receive timely treatment due to spotty insurance coverage and a shortage of local specialists, according to research and interviews with more than a dozen eating disorder researchers, doctors, dietitians, therapists, policy advocates, and mothers.

title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
summary: 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping this weekend, according to the National Retail Federation
text:
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.
But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.
Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.
After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.
"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.
If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).
These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.
Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.

title: Opinion: Montana’s ‘right to try’ law makes patients responsible for bearing costs — and risks
summary: Montana has become the first state to have its own ‘right to try’ law, but important questions remain, researchers write.
text:
In July, Montana became the first state to license clinics to offer patients who are not terminally ill drugs and devices that the Food and Drug Administration has not approved. Supporters call state Senate bill 535 a first-in-the-nation expansion of the “right to try.” Critics say it lets patients, including medical tourists from other states, pay out of pocket for unproven therapies. They are both right, in different ways. While the expansion of access to experimental treatments may provide patients with hope, the risks that patients may pay high costs for ineffective and even unsafe treatments remain high.
The goal is to expand access to experimental therapies, with stem cell, anti-aging therapies, and biologics being likely use cases. But the law leaves major questions unanswered: How much will patients pay? Who will bear the cost if complications arise later? And, because these therapies are being used outside a rigorous research setting, how will anyone know whether they actually work?
For patients, a primary concern is likely to be cost. SB535 makes patients financially responsible for the experimental treatment — with the price set by the company supplying the drug or device. The required patient agreement must describe “all the anticipated costs” of the treatment itself. But patients will likely face additional costs, including travel to Montana for those out of state, and follow-up care.
Patients are also, in theory, responsible to pay out of pocket for medical care related to any complications — they are not supposed to go through their insurance companies. But how will insurers determine if a medical problem stems from an experimental treatment? That’s left ambiguous by the law. Long-term medical effects will be particularly hard to trace, especially if a product hasn’t yet had robust safety testing and documentation of its long-term side effects. Thus, care for complications may fall on patients, or it may be paid by insurers who had no say in the use of an experimental treatment.
And how are people to judge whether a treatment is worth its price? For approved therapies, there’s trial data on survival rates, plus continued post-market study. These data help clarify the expected benefits for specific patients. SB535 does not require companies to conduct comparable analyses, nor are companies bound to set prices with any value framework in mind.
Proponents of SB535 argue that skipping costly trials will lower development costs and, eventually, prices. However, if companies wish to generate evidence for conventional FDA approval, they will need to go beyond the requirements in SB535. If they fail to collect detailed patient characteristics such as history of disease and patient demographics, it will be hard to determine how the drug might work in a larger patient population. title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
summary: Constantly buying new things can be problematic, says journalist Eric Athas, author of the new book "Saying No to New." Here's how to break the cycle and find joy in what you already have.
text:
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?
Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.
To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?
Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.
If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.
There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.
What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?
New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.
But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.
These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?
Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions. These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.
For example, at the checkout page of a website or an app, there might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.
The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.
What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?
Expand what I call "the new-thing gap." That's the time and distance bet

title: The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills
summary: RSPCA hands out food, vet vouchers, cat litter and toys to pet owners struggling with bills.
text:
The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills
- Published
At Burngreave Foodbank in Sheffield, a queue of worried people are here not to collect groceries for themselves, but food for their pets.
The RSPCA has launched a pop-up food bank to hand out cat litter, veterinary vouchers and pet toys as well as food.
Many of the dog and cat owners using the service say that rising bills are leaving them in fear they will not be able to care for their beloved companions.
John Paul Feely, 59, has four cats and a dog, and currently spends £35 a month on them.
"At the moment we're facing rises in fuel costs, food costs and you've got to make a choice at some point, can we look after the animals?" he says.
Feely worries that unexpected vet bills as well as the day-to-day expenses could tip him over the edge when his energy bill goes up in January.
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.
A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year.
The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
Feely lives with his partner and explains that they are already making tough decisions about "turning the lights out and not putting the heating on".
He is able to take home food supplies and a dog chew toy.
As food bank volunteers offer tea and coffee to those waiting in the queue, Angela Gillot accepts a small dog jacket from the RSPCA stall with a smile.
She explains with a tear in her eye that since becoming unemployed she has felt the pinch of rising bills.
The RSPCA estimates that the cost of keeping a small dog like a Jack Russell could be up to £209 a month.
Energy costs going up next year "will affect everything," Gillot admits, as she describes how she and her dog huddle up under a blanket to keep warm.
"We do love these pets. We're a pet-loving nation aren't we? But it's getting harder.
"When I got my dogs I was working, so I try my best, but the price of food, especially what's of quality, I just really can't afford it.
"It's not often you go to these places and they think about your pets," the 58-year-old says.
Tricia Watts, the upbeat assistant manger at Burngreave Foodbank, is enthusiastic about the support from the RSPCA.
She explains that while the food bank works with people in food poverty, it cannot always help people with animal care as it relies on donations.
She has seen demand increase, and donations fall, in the seven years she has worked at the food bank.
"I think pets are so important to people. If people are going through hard times, they're still important and they don't want to lose them."
Growing bills are of particular concern to exotic animal owners as many birds, reptiles and fish must be kept in carefully maintained conditions that are often energy-intensive.

title: In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs
summary: Researchers engineered a protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs, raising hopes of one day improving IVF outcomes
text:
Around the world, people are increasingly choosing to have babies later in life for reasons both social and economic. As they get older though, they face a mounting biological challenge: genetic errors caused by chromosomes failing to separate correctly. This phenomenon, known as aneuploidy, is the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles, and miscarriage, and it increases dramatically around the age of 40. Studies have shown that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities.
One of the main drivers of aneuploidy is the loss of a protein complex called cohesin, which acts like a molecular glue holding chromosomes together. In a new study, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, engineered a novel protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs. The study, published Thursday in Science, raises the possibility of one day developing such a system into a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in human eggs used for IVF.
“There is still work ahead, but their proof of concept was highly successful,” said Rajiv McCoy, a biologist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the work. McCoy’s lab is focused on pregnancy loss, the leading cause of which is aneuploidy. It is estimated that about half of all human conceptions are lost before birth, including the roughly 15% of known pregnancies that end in miscarriage. Technologies that could reduce the odds of miscarriage and expand women’s biological reproductive windows by addressing aneuploidy would have far-reaching consequences for the IVF industry and for society at large. “The stakes are very high,” McCoy said.
When a cell prepares to divide, its chromosomes replicate, forming two copies, or sister chromatids, that are all lined up and organized by a cellular winch system known as the spindle. Within the spindle, the sister chromatids are tethered to each other by cohesin — its ring-like structure traps DNA from both sisters inside it. In most cells, cohesin only has to do this work for a few hours before other enzymes cleave it apart, freeing the chromatids to separate into two new cells. But in oocytes, cohesin has to keep this bond going for decades.
That’s because female babies are born with all the oocytes they will ever have. And already at birth, those 1 to 2 million immature egg cells have begun to divide, and the cohesin’s job is only finished when fertilization occurs. That triggers the end of the division process called meiosis in which the egg cells eject half their genetic material so they can fuse with sperm to make an embryo.
Over all that time, the cohesin molecule doesn’t seem to be reloaded, said Melina Schuh, a director at the Max Planck Institute who led the new work.

title: Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
summary: Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.
text:
Nvidia's board under fire for handling of CEO's alleged affairs
Even as Jensen Huang has returned to work, Nvidia's board is facing criticism over how it handled the crisis brought on by the CEO's alleged affairs.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
How did a board that unanimously decided that its CEO must go decide a few days later to bring him right back? We're talking about Nvidia and its founder, former and now current CEO Jensen Huang. NPR's Andrea Hsu has been gathering reaction to the board's handling of the crisis, and she's with us now to tell us more.
Good morning, Andrea.
ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: Good morning.
MARTIN: OK, so let me just point out here that at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, Huang apologized for hurting his family and violating the company's code of conduct. That's according to a livestream of the meeting which was viewed by The New York Times. He also reportedly said that President Trump didn't pressure the board into bringing him back. NPR has reached out to Nvidia for confirmation of this, but hasn't heard back. You've been hearing from people who know how boards are meant to operate. What are you hearing from them?
HSU: Yeah. Well, there's been criticism from both those who think Jensen Huang shouldn't have been brought back and also those who think it was the right thing to do. And, Michel, let's remember the role of boards - they exist to make informed and deliberate decisions that are in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. In many instances, they are the only mechanism of accountability for companies and CEOs. And in the case of Nvidia, you know, a lot of people say the board fell short on these duties, and we've asked Nvidia for a response to that, but we haven't heard back on that, either.
MARTIN: Now, recognizing that you're getting a range of opinions there, do these experts have thoughts on what should have happened?
HSU: Yeah. Well, many are saying that the board should have made different choices. Our colleague Shannon Bond spoke with Rob Lalka. He's a professor at Tulane's Freeman School of Business (ph), and he points out that in the last decade, there have been a number of high-profile cases similar to what allegedly happened at Nvidia - you know, a CEO having an affair with an employee. It happened at Intel, McDonald's, Nestle. And Lalka says those boards followed their policies, and those CEOs were out. They decided it had to happen to preserve company values and credibility. But then, as for Nvidia, here's what Lalka says.
ROB LALKA: The board basically went around its entire process that it had set in place for that investigation to put him back into power.
MARTIN: But you also mentioned that there are people who think bringing Huang back was the right thing to do. Say more about that.

title: STAT+: The grueling struggle to find a primary care doctor in the ‘medical capital’ of America
summary: Boston is supposed to be the medical capital of America. Yet many don’t have primary care access, hurting their ability to get treatments, screenings, and medical advice.
text:
I was three days into calling doctors’ offices, trying to get a primary care appointment. Over and over, I sat on hold, only to hear I’d have to wait weeks or months. It was mind numbing.
Then I reached a voicemail greeting that sounded about as despondent as I felt.
“We’ve received an extremely high volume of messages due to multiple providers in our area retiring or leaving their practice very recently,” the woman’s voice said with a hint of exasperation, “so please understand it may take longer than normal to receive a return call back.”

title: From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
summary: Networks of plumbers and electricians are scamming people on a large scale, the BBC reveals.
text:
From £250 job to £9,000 bill: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
- Published
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.
Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.
"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.
The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.
The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.
In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".
In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.
"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.
One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.
After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".
Trading Standards said the average rogue trader call-out scam now costs the victim about £10,000.
The impact can be devastating.
Clive, who lives in London, is undergoing treatment for cancer.
He said he had felt forced to pay the rogue trader who came to his home and charged £9,153 for installing an outdoor socket to fit garden lights he already owned.
An independent electrical expert told the BBC the job had not been done properly, was left in an unsafe state and should have cost no more than £250.
Clive said he no longer feels safe in his home.
He explained how he had searched for a local electrician on Google when his usual tradesperson was unavailable and came across Chriss Electrician Ltd.
Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.
"I was shocked," said Clive.
He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.
He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.
Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.
"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.
"When people come to the door now, I think, 'Oh God, who's that?' I don't feel safe any more."
